articles.title: Raspberry Pi Projects Can Be Affordable Again with Budget-Friendly Options
articles.summary: A budget-friendly Raspberry Pi option can be had for just $45 and can handle several simple projects without any issues.
articles.content: Raspberry Pi projects often fizzle out before completion due to lack of dedication and patience from beginners. These fun and useful ideas can help prevent your Raspberry Pi build from gathering dust on a shelf somewhere. A 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 now costs $385, which is over three times its original price tag. This steep increase is part of the ongoing RAM crisis affecting data centers worldwide. The rising cost has made it no longer an impulse purchase that it once was. Mini PCs have also been impacted by the RAM shortage, but they are still worth considering for some projects due to their speed and performance in running regular PC software. The 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 can be had for just $45 and can handle several of the simple projects listed below without any issues. This budget-friendly option is a great way to get started with your Raspberry Pi, even if you're not planning on using it for demanding tasks. A clever solution to tackle ad blockers across multiple devices in your home is to create a network-wide ad blocker using a Raspberry Pi. This approach eliminates the need for installing ad blockers on each individual device, which can be a tedious task. The software used to block ads and trackers relies on publicly available lists of known ad servers and trackers. To get started with this project, you simply plug your Pi directly into your router using an Ethernet cable, making it easy to set up even for beginners. However, the Pi needs a fixed IP address and some configuration tweaks to ensure that it functions properly as a DNS server on your network. Once these steps are taken care of, the Pi can effectively block ads and trackers across all devices connected to the same network. The simplicity of this project has made it one of the most popular entry points for beginners exploring Raspberry Pi projects. With its ease of setup and clear objectives, it's an ideal starting point for those looking to get hands-on experience with their Pi. To turn your Raspberry Pi into a fully functional media center, you'll need a few extra components beyond the microSD and board itself. These include a game controller, power supply, and video cable - typically micro HDMI to HDMI. The type of games you can play on this setup is also worth noting: since the software doesn't come with built-in games, you'll need to provide your own ROMs, which may require navigating some legal gray areas. A more ambitious project that still uses a Raspberry Pi as its core is building a retro gaming handheld. However, creating one from scratch can be quite complex and might not be feasible for beginners - especially considering the availability of pre-made options at relatively affordable prices. For those who don't want to venture into streaming services, this setup has another use: playing back movies, shows, music, and photos you already own on your digital media library. A software like LibreELEC can boot your Pi into Kodi, a user-friendly interface for accessing your content. Kodi allows you to organize your files from a hard drive or home server, filling in artwork and episode info automatically as it goes along. There are also free community-built add-ons available to customize the experience further - and with HDMI-CEC, you can even control Kodi using your TV's remote. The Raspberry Pi can be used to recreate a popular feature of Google's discontinued Chromecast Audio. This small device was designed to turn any ordinary speaker into a wireless one by plugging it into an audio input. It essentially made speakers that couldn't stream music independently, capable of doing so. To set up the Pi as a wireless speaker, you need to plug it into your old stereo or powered speakers and install Raspotify for Spotify Connect or Shairport Sync for AirPlay. These programs allow you to use the Pi as an audio output option in Spotify's device list or on your iPhone through AirPlay. This way, you can stream music from these platforms directly to your speaker. It's worth noting that this project is not meant to be confused with a regular Chromecast, which was designed specifically for video streaming and has since been replaced by the Google TV Streamer. The Raspberry Pi's functionality is more similar to that of the discontinued Chromecast Audio, which was designed for audio streaming only. The Raspberry Pi can also be used as a client for modern PC games, allowing you to play them from the comfort of your couch. A project called Sunshine enables local streaming of PC games, making it possible to use your existing library on your TV without needing a separate gaming console. This solution is less expensive than buying a dedicated Steam Link box. Sunshine works by setting up the Raspberry Pi as a client for your PC's games, allowing you to stream them directly to your TV. This project is not meant to replace a full-fledged gaming system like the Steam Machine, but it does provide an affordable way to access your existing game library on your big screen. To get started with Sunshine and Moonlight, you need to install the former on a PC and its companion software on a Raspberry Pi. This setup is compatible with NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, and it's free of charge. The pairing process involves linking the two devices with a PIN, after which you can enjoy your PC gaming library on the big screen. However, for a seamless experience, it's recommended to connect both the PC and the Pi via wired connections. While Wi-Fi is an option, Ethernet provides a more reliable connection for local streaming. This ensures that your games run smoothly without any interruptions or lag. The Raspberry Pi 500 is another simple project that can be used as a child's first computer. It's essentially a Pi built into a keyboard and comes with a basic desktop setup that includes a web browser and coding tools. Plugging it into a monitor gets you started, but its price of $180 might not be the most attractive option. While the Raspberry Pi 500 provides a solid foundation for learning, it doesn't come with parental controls out of the box. This means you'll need to set up controls before letting your child use it unsupervised, especially if they're going to be using it independently. articles.title: Parenting Style Influenced by Large Family Upbringing
articles.summary: The author's childhood experience in a large family influenced their parenting style, which emphasizes compromise, generosity, and empathy.
articles.content: As a child of parents who married young and were still navigating adulthood themselves, I was part of a large family that was often chaotic but always loving. My three siblings and I had to learn to share space and resources, which taught us valuable lessons about compromise and generosity. Growing up in this environment also meant there was less individual attention from our parents, who were stretched thin trying to care for their young children. This scarcity of one-on-one time didn't seem to matter, however, as the love that flowed through our household came from multiple directions at once. When I became a stepmom myself at 25, I drew on this upbringing to inform my parenting style. Growing up in a large family taught me valuable lessons about human nature that have stayed with me to this day. My parents were responsible for making the rules and setting boundaries, but we children were also expected to look out for one another. Older siblings naturally took on a mentorship role, often unintentionally, as they navigated their own childhood challenges alongside ours. In our household, younger siblings learned quickly that it was essential to keep up with the rest of us in order to avoid being left behind. We witnessed each other's mistakes and heartbreaks firsthand, which taught me about empathy and compassion from a young age. This experience laid the groundwork for my understanding of human behavior, an education I would draw upon later as a parent myself. As I grew older and started a family of my own, I applied these lessons to my parenting style. Our four children, ranging in age from 16 to 32, have given me the opportunity to see how the world has changed over time. Parenting today is vastly different from what it was when I first started out in the late 1990s. Raising multiple children at once can be chaotic, with each child requiring individual attention and care. In a large family like ours, it's not always possible to give every child equal amounts of time and focus. However, my upbringing taught me how to observe and understand the needs of those around me, a skill that has proven invaluable as a parent. Growing up in a large family taught me that every child has unique needs and circumstances. In my household, it was often the quiet ones who required extra attention and care. As a parent, I've learned to look beyond what my children say and observe the subtle changes in their behavior. This skill has been invaluable in understanding what each of them truly requires from me. One child may thrive on lengthy conversations at midnight, while another needs space before opening up. Conversely, a rule that motivates one child can be suffocating for another. I've come to realize that consistency is essential, but rigidity is not always the best approach. This understanding has been shaped by my own experiences growing up in a family with five siblings. Each of us had distinct experiences and personalities, despite sharing parents and a home. Birth order, individual circumstances, and personality traits all contributed to our diverse childhoods. As a parent, I've applied this insight to understand that each of my children has their own unique experience within our family. As parents, it's natural to feel like every decision we make will have a lasting impact on our child's life. I recall feeling this way with my first child, where every milestone seemed monumental and every setback felt catastrophic. However, as the years went by and I had more children, I began to realize that life is unpredictable and things can change rapidly. What may seem like an insurmountable problem today might be resolved on its own tomorrow. This experience taught me to prioritize my concerns and intervene only when truly necessary. Raising four children also taught me the importance of being a supportive partner in parenting. With multiple kids, it's easy for disagreements and frustration to arise, but I learned that supporting each other through these challenges is crucial. By doing so, we became stronger as a couple and better equipped to navigate the ups and downs of parenthood. As I look back on my experience, I'm reminded that being a good parent isn't about trying to control every aspect of your child's life. It's about knowing when to step in and when to let things unfold naturally, and trusting that your children will learn and grow from their experiences, even if they make mistakes along the way. Parenting is not about providing identical experiences for each child, but rather adapting to their unique needs and personalities. At 25, I was a perfectionist mother who sought to prevent every mistake from occurring, whereas at 52, I've come to realize that mistakes often serve as valuable learning opportunities. This shift in perspective has allowed me to be more flexible and open-minded in my approach to parenting. As a child of six siblings myself, I learned early on about the importance of adapting and evolving with each new situation. Now, as a mother of four, I see that this same principle applies to raising children, sometimes it's necessary to pivot and try new approaches, even if they don't work for every child or in every circumstance. Raising multiple children requires an incredible amount of flexibility, patience, and understanding, but it also allows for growth and development on both the parent's and child's part.
